title: Compose email and password validators from named rules

blocks.text: Validation reads best as small, named `Predicate`s joined with `and()`. Each rule can be tested alone, and because `and()` short-circuits like `&&`, a rule placed after a null check never sees `null`.
Write two methods in `Validators`, each returning a composed `Predicate<String>`:

items: `email()` accepts text that is not null or empty, contains `@` with at least one character before it, and has a `.` somewhere after the `@` with at least one character between the two.
`strongPassword()` accepts text of at least 8 characters with an upper-case letter, a lower-case letter, a digit and a character that is neither a letter nor a digit.

blocks.text: Either predicate may be handed `null`. Check the page's own examples against each rule's exact wording.

cases.says: A well-formed email and a strong password pass; plainly bad ones fail.
A null email or password is simply invalid; the null check comes first so nothing throws.
An email that starts with @ has no local part and is invalid.
The domain needs text, then a dot: user@example and user@.com are invalid.
A password missing any one rule (length, upper, lower, digit, other) fails.

concepts: Named rules joined with and() make a validator whose parts can each be tested alone.
Putting the null check first in an and() chain keeps every later check safe from null.
